history.dynasty: Jaintia Kingdom (established under Jaintia kings; built in the 16th-17th century during the reigns of Dhan Manik and Jaso Manik)
history.period: 16th-17th century (about 500-600 years old per local tradition)
history.summary: FLAG ON CSV TOWN: the temple is at Nartiang village in West Jaintia Hills district, NOT Mairang (Mairang is in Eastern West Khasi Hills, far to the west) - the CSV town is wrong. Nartiang was the summer capital of the Jaintia Kingdom, and its Durga temple is one of the 51 Shakti Peethas (the Shakti worshipped as 'Jayanti', Bhairava as 'Kamadishwar'), believed to mark where Sati's left thigh fell; the goddess is locally known as Jainteshwari. King Dhan Manik (1596-1612) made Nartiang his summer capital; his successor Jaso Manik (1606-1641) married Lakshmi Narayana, daughter of the Hindu Koch king Nara Narayana, whose influence is credited with bringing Shaktism to the Jaintia royalty. Legend says the goddess appeared to Jaso Manik in a dream and asked him to build the temple. The shrine began as a simple stone-and-wood structure with a thatched roof in Khasi style; the Ramakrishna Mission later redeveloped it with a tin roof and a more permanent structure (verify). It stands on a hilltop overlooking the Myntdu (Myundu) river, with a 'Boli Garbha' (sacrificial pit) in the basement connected by a tunnel to the river; ancient cannons of the Jaintia kings are kept on the premises, suggesting the site was part of a royal fort. Worship uniquely blends Hindu and Khasi-Jaintia traditions - the deity is a decorated plantain trunk, not an idol - and the local Syiem (chieftain) remains the temple's chief patron; the present priests are direct descendants of the original priests from Jaintiapur. Human sacrifice is said to have been practised here until the 19th century (verify - now replaced by goat sacrifice). The Central Puja Committee of Meghalaya maintains the temple; in 2017 the Union government announced it would be declared a heritage site (verify current status). Nartiang is also famed as the 'Garden of Monoliths' - clusters of menhirs (Moo Shynrang) and dolmens (Moo Kynthai), some erected around 1500 AD, including the 8-metre Moo Long Syiem.

name: Nartiang Durga Temple
town_description: Nartiang is a historic village in West Jaintia Hills district, about 60-65 km east of Shillong on the Shillong-Jowai road. Once the summer capital of the Jaintia Kingdom, it is famous as the 'Garden of Monoliths' - scattered clusters of ancient Khasi-Jaintia menhirs and dolmens - and for the Nartiang Durga Temple, one of the 51 Shakti Peethas. Nearby attractions include Thadlaskein Lake and the district town of Jowai (~25 km).

travel.airport: Nearest airport with scheduled commercial flights: Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport, Guwahati, Assam (approx. 170-200 km by road; verify). Shillong (Umroi) airport is closer (approx. 85-95 km; verify) but has limited scheduled services (verify).
travel.railway: Guwahati railway station is the nearest major railhead (approx. 165-190 km by road; verify); onward by taxi or bus via Shillong/Jowai.
travel.road: Nartiang is approx. 60-65 km east of Shillong on the Shillong-Jowai road (NH-6) and approx. 25 km from Jowai (verify); reachable by taxi, shared sumo, and state buses from Shillong and Jowai.

visitor_information.best_time: October to March for pleasant weather. Durga Puja (September-October) is the most significant and vibrant time to visit, though crowded with pilgrims from across the Northeast.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Approx. 7:00 AM to 8:00 PM daily per traveller listings (verify - temple-managed hours are not published). No entry fee reported (verify). Dress modestly; the shrine follows Khasi-Jaintia customs alongside Hindu ritual.
